payload.ratio: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties under Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act merely because the driver of a light motor vehicle did not have a specific endorsement on their licence to drive it as a commercial vehicle.

payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Court held that where a driving license is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period of the accident, but directed the insurance company to satisfy the award and recover the amount from the insured owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.
payload.ratio: When an application for renewal of a driving license is made more than 30 days after its expiry, the license is renewed from the date of renewal; thus, the driver does not hold a valid license on the date of an accident occurring during the lapsed period, absolving the insurer of primary liability, though a 'pay and recover' order may be issued in favour of third-party claimants.

payload.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
payload.holding: The court held that the insurance companies were jointly and severally liable with the owners to satisfy the third-party claims despite the drivers' licences not being current on the exact date of the accidents, and enhanced the compensation awarded in both claim cases while reducing the interest rate to 9% per annum.

established the natural consequences have to flow.
In view of the above analysis the following situations emerge:
1. The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than
third party risks.
2. Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent
fatality.
3 In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover
the same from the insured.
4. The concept of purposive interpretation has no application to cases relatable to Section 149 of the
Act.
The High Courts/Commissions shall now consider the matter afresh in the light of the position in
law as delineated above.
The appeals are allowed as aforesaid with no order as to costs.

contract of insurance by cogent evidence. In the event the Insurance Company fails to
prove that there has been breach of conditions of the policy on the part of the
insured, the Insurance Company cannot be absolved of its liability. This Court did not
lay down a degree of proof, but held that the parties alleging the breach must be held
to have succeeded in establishing the breach of the condition of the contract of

The Tribunal, must arrive at a finding on the basis of the materials available on the

In para 110 also the summary of the findings were recorded which reads as follows:
(i) Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 providing compulsory insurance of
vehicles against third-party risks is a social welfare legislation to extend relief by
compensation to victims of accidents caused by use of motor vehicles. The provisions
of compulsory insurance coverage of all vehicles are with this paramount object and
the provisions of the Act have to be so interpreted as to effectuate the said object.
(ii) An insurer is entitled to raise a defence in a claim petition filed under Section
163-A or Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, inter alia, in terms of Section

149(2)(a)(ii) of the said Act.
(iii) The breach of policy condition e.g. disqualification of the driver or invalid driving
licence of the driver, as contained in sub-
section (2)(a)(ii) of Section 149, has to be proved to have been committed by the insured for
avoiding liability by the insurer. Mere absence, fake or invalid driving licence or disqualification of
the driver for driving at the relevant time, are not in themselves defences available to the insurer
against either the insured or the third parties.

args.question: What must an owner do to check a driver's licence before employing them, and does failing to check defeat the insurer's defence?

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to make enquiries with RTOs across the country to verify authenticity. If the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held an LMV licence with a 'transport vehicle' endorsement. The owner remained ex parte, so no evidence was led on what checks he performed. The court held that when a driver produces a licence with an endorsement to drive 'transport vehicle', the owner is not expected to verify further details.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most authoritative statement in the corpus on the standard of care expected of an owner when checking a driver's licence. It directly quotes Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338 and Swaran Singh, establishing that the owner's duty is limited to a facial check — not a forensic investigation.
supporting.quote: When an owner is hiring a driver he will therefore have to check whether the driver has a driving licence. If the driver produces a driving licence which on the face of it looks genuine, the owner is not expected to find out whether the licence has in fact been issued by a competent authority or not. ... Thus where the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently there would be no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).

supporting.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
supporting.principle: An insurer cannot avoid its statutory liability to pay third-party compensation merely because the driver of an LMV did not have a specific endorsement to drive it as a commercial vehicle. The third party's right to recover from the insurer is statutory and cannot be defeated by licence endorsement technicalities.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held a valid LMV licence but lacked a commercial endorsement to drive a Mahindra Maxi Cab (a transport vehicle). The Supreme Court reversed the High Court and held the insurer liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: This Supreme Court authority limits the scope of the insurer's defence: where the driver holds a licence for the class of vehicle (LMV), the absence of a specific endorsement for commercial use is not a ground to avoid third-party liability. This supports the argument that minor licence deficiencies do not defeat the claim.
supporting.quote: Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

supporting.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
supporting.principle: Non-renewal of an otherwise valid driving licence on the date of the accident does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer of third-party liability. The breach must be wilful and must have contributed to the accident.
supporting.fact_alignment: The drivers held valid licences that had expired shortly before the accident and were renewed afterwards. The court held this was not a fundamental breach because the non-renewal did not contribute to causing the accident.
supporting.why_it_matters: This judgment distinguishes between 'no licence at all' and 'licence expired but later renewed'. It supports the argument that even if the owner failed to check the licence's current validity, the breach may not be fundamental enough to defeat the insurer's defence — the insurer still pays and recovers.
supporting.quote: The non-renewal of the licence as on the date of the accident cannot be said to have contributed to the causing of the accident. Where the breach alleged is not a factor which has contributed to the causing of the accident, the said breach would not be a fundamental breach so as to afford a ground to the insurer to avoid liability altogether.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Even where the insurer proves a fundamental breach under Section 149(2), the insurer remains bound to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured. The insurer's liability to the third party is statutory and cannot be escaped.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench decision consolidating the law: the insurer must pay the third party first and then recover from the insured, regardless of whether the breach is proved.
supporting.why_it_matters: This confirms that even if the owner failed to check the licence (and the insurer proves breach), the insurer's defence does not result in the third party going uncompensated. The remedy is pay-and-recover, not avoidance of liability.
supporting.quote: Even if there is any violation or breach of condition of a policy, the insurer has to discharge the initial burden of proving the grounds taken under Section 149(2) of the Act. In spite of that, the insurer has to indemnify the amount and can recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: The insurer's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory. Even if the insurer proves a conscious breach of policy terms (invalid licence), it is entitled only to recovery rights against the owner/driver, not to avoid payment to the third party.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver and owner did not challenge the finding of breach. The court confirmed the pay-and-recover order.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces that the insurer's defence (even if successful on the merits of breach) results in pay-and-recover, not exoneration from third-party liability.
supporting.quote: The liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy. The insurer is not liable to indemnify the owner, though it must pay the third party and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that the owner's failure to ensure the driver had a licence is a fundamental breach. The tribunal held that the owner's non-production of the driver's licence, coupled with the charge sheet stating the driver had no licence, proved breach. They will argue this shows the owner's failure to check is itself the breach.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable because the owner did not produce the driver's licence at all and the charge sheet itself stated the driver had no licence. Where the owner has checked and the driver produced a licence that appears genuine on its face, the standard from Lehru (cited in doc_027) applies — the owner is not expected to conduct a forensic verification. Additionally, even here the court ordered pay-and-recover, not outright exoneration.
adverse.quote: It is held that the respondent No.1 has breached the fundamental condition of the policy by allowing the driver who has no driving licence to drive the vehicle.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
adverse.principle: Where a driver holds only an LMV licence without the specific authorisation/badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions. The insurer must pay the third party and recover from the insured owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that the owner bears responsibility for ensuring the driver has the correct class of licence and any required badge/endorsement. The court found breach because the driver lacked a badge for a tourist maxi cab, and the owner was held liable to reimburse the insurer.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover — the insurer paid the third party. The owner's liability was to reimburse, not to bear the third-party claim directly. Moreover, the court's finding of breach was based on the specific regulatory requirements (Tamil Nadu Motor Vehicles Rules) for badge endorsements, which may not apply in all jurisdictions. The owner's duty is to check the licence on its face; if the licence appears to cover the vehicle class, the owner is not expected to know every regulatory nuance.
adverse.quote: The absence of any endorsement in the driving licence as to the issuance of authorisation to drive the transport vehicle and non-mention of allotment of badge number clearly shows that the 3rd Respondent was not in possession of a valid driving licence.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
adverse.principle: For driving a goods carriage carrying dangerous/hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving licence is mandatory under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules. The absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that the owner has a statutory duty under Rule 132(5) of the CMVR to ensure the driver holds the correct endorsement for the specific type of goods being carried. This extends the owner's verification duty beyond just checking for a valid licence.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is limited to vehicles carrying dangerous/hazardous goods (tankers), which have specific additional regulatory requirements under Rules 9 and 132 of the CMVR. For ordinary goods vehicles or passenger vehicles, no such special endorsement is required. The owner's duty in the general case is limited to checking that the driver holds a licence for the class of vehicle.
adverse.quote: As per Rule 132 (5) of Central Motor Vehicle Rule, 1989, it is the duty of the owner to ensure that the driver of the goods carriage carrying dangerous or hazardous goods holds a driving license as per the rule 9 of the aforesaid Central Motor Vehicles Rules.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
adverse.principle: Where a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum. The driver did not hold a valid licence on the accident date, and the insurer is entitled to pay and recover.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that the owner should have checked that the licence was currently valid (not expired) at the time of employment/accident. The owner's failure to check the expiry date is a breach.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: The court still ordered pay-and-recover — the third party was compensated. The owner's liability was to reimburse. Moreover, the owner's duty is to check the licence on its face; if the licence shows a validity period that appears current, the owner is not expected to independently verify with the RTO whether it has been cancelled or expired. The breach here was the driver's failure to renew in time, not the owner's failure to check.
adverse.quote: The liability fastened on the Insurance Company is contrary to law. The Tribunal ought to have fastened the liability on the owner of the vehicle, who entrusted the vehicle to a person, who did not possess valid and effective driving license as on the date of accident.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: Swaran Singh's principles apply only to third-party claims, not own-damage claims. A fake driving licence cannot be cured by subsequent renewal.
adverse.risk_to_client: The opposing side will cite this to argue that where the licence is fake (not merely expired or lacking an endorsement), the owner's failure to detect the fake licence is a more serious breach. They will argue that the owner should have been more diligent.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case expressly limits its holding to own-damage claims (non-third-party). For third-party claims (which is the context of the present question), Swaran Singh applies and the insurer must pay and recover. Moreover, the standard from Lehru (cited in doc_027) is that if the licence looks genuine on its face, the owner is not expected to detect a fake. The burden is on the insurer to prove the owner knew or noticed the licence was fake.
adverse.quote: The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks.

priority_arguments: The owner's duty is limited to checking whether the driver produces a licence that appears genuine on its face and covers the class of vehicle being driven (Lehru principle, cited in doc_027). The owner is not expected to make enquiries with RTOs or detect sophisticated forgeries.

Even if the insurer proves a breach (e.g., no valid licence, expired licence, missing endorsement), the insurer's statutory liability to the third party remains. The remedy is pay-and-recover, not avoidance (docs_025, 033, 035).

The breach must be 'fundamental' — i.e., it must have contributed to the cause of the accident. Non-renewal of an expired licence or a missing endorsement that did not cause the accident is not a fundamental breach (doc_034).

The burden of proving breach is on the insurer. The insurer must prove not just that the licence was invalid, but that the owner was guilty of negligence or wilful breach (doc_025, citing Swaran Singh).
Where the driver held a licence for the class of vehicle (e.g., LMV) but lacked a commercial endorsement, the insurer cannot avoid third-party liability (doc_032 — S.Iyyapan, Supreme Court).
strategy.compensation_range: Not applicable — the question concerns liability/defence, not quantum.
risks: If the owner made no effort at all to check the driver's licence (e.g., hired a driver without asking for any licence), the tribunal may find a fundamental breach. However, even then the remedy is pay-and-recover, not denial of the third-party claim.
If the licence is fake and the insurer can prove the owner knew or had notice it was fake, the insurer may avoid liability even to the third party (Lehru caveat). This is a high bar for the insurer.

For vehicles carrying hazardous goods (tankers), additional regulatory duties are cast on the owner under Rule 132(5) CMVR to ensure the driver holds a special endorsement (doc_001). This is a narrow exception.

In own-damage claims (not third-party), Swaran Singh does not apply and a fake licence can defeat the claim entirely (doc_031). This is irrelevant to third-party claims but relevant if the insurer has a separate own-damage defence.
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: In third-party claims, the insurer should always seek a pay-and-recover order rather than resisting liability outright. The consistent position across the corpus is that the insurer must satisfy the award and recover from the insured owner if breach is proved. The insurer's defence (failure to check licence) goes to recovery rights, not to avoidance of third-party liability.

caveats: This corpus does not contain the full text of National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 or United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Lehru (2003) 3 SCC 338, which are the foundational Supreme Court authorities on this issue. However, these cases are extensively cited and quoted in the corpus judgments (particularly doc_027, doc_025, doc_033, doc_031), so their principles are reliably extracted.

The corpus contains no judgment where the insurer successfully avoided all liability to a third party solely on the ground that the owner failed to check the driver's licence. The consistent outcome across all relevant judgments is pay-and-recover.

doc_031 (Laxmi Narain Dhut) is an own-damage case and its ratio is expressly limited to non-third-party claims. It is included in adverse only because opposing counsel may attempt to extend its reasoning; the distinction is clean.

payload.holding: The High Court held that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation for the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle, dismissed the owners' appeal regarding negligence and quantum, and dismissed the claimants' cross-objections for enhancement.
payload.ratio: Where a passenger travelling in a goods vehicle is a gratuitous passenger whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered under Section 95 of the Motor Vehicles Act and is not covered by the terms of the insurance policy, the insurer cannot be held liable for compensation.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: The owner's duty is to check whether the driver produces a licence that on the face of it looks genuine. The owner is not expected to make enquiries with RTOs across the country to verify authenticity. If the owner has satisfied himself that the driver has a licence and is driving competently, there is no breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii).
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver held an LMV licence with a 'transport vehicle' endorsement. The owner remained ex parte, so no evidence was led on what checks he performed. The court held that when a driver produces a licence with an endorsement to drive 'transport vehicle', the owner is not expected to verify further details.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most authoritative statement in the corpus on the standard of care expected of an owner when checking a driver's licence.
